newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Experts sound warning of world water shortage.
newsitem.headline: Experts sound warning of world water shortage.

text.p: International experts said on Friday that dwindling water supplies could provoke armed conflicts, especially in the Middle East and Africa, unless action was taken now.
They spoke as a World Water Forum opened in the southern Moroccan city of Marrakesh, gathering specialists, bankers, and senior officials from 50 countries.

"Scarce water resources can lead to further competition and risks of domestic and international conflicts," said Ismail Sirageldin, head of the Stockholm-based non-governmental organisation Global Water Partnership.
The Middle East and Africa topped the list of "hot regions" which would be linked to water disputes in future, he said.
A senior U.N. official, Pierre Najlis, said: "For most of the world, the current pattern of water resource development and utilisation is not sustainable.
"Unless action is taken now, the situation will become increasingly serious in the future," he said.
Najlis, chief of the U.N. energy and natural resources department, said recent studies showed water resources were a key factor in sustainable development.

"By the year 2025, as much as two-thirds of the (world) population in the lower income categories could be facing moderate to severe water stress, and 35 percent of the same population could be facing severe stress as compared to about nine percent in 1995," Najlis said.
According to U.N. estimates, 77 percent of the world's people live in countries with a per capita income of less than $2,895, with most of this group on less than $795 per year.

The Marrakesh meeting coinciding with U.N. World Water Day will examine the outlook for world water supplies and ways of managing them. The experts, including U.N., World Bank, non-government agencies and development banks, will assess the main problems, including energy, environment, health, food security and climatic changes.
Bo Kjellen, from the Swedish environment ministry, said poor people often paid more their water than those better off.

"Furthermore, poor women literally carry the burden of this situation, since they are mostly responsible for water supply in villages and remote areas," Kjellen said, adding that the only solution was "water-use planning" and "full participation at local level".
Morocco's Public Works Minister Abdelaziz Meziane told the forum that increasing populations meant "many countries will face a serious problem of water resources in the 21st Century".
In the next decade, water would represent "the same value" as crude oil and be a source of conflicts, he said.
UNESCO Director-General Federico Mayor, who will open the second day's session, said in a statement that water would be one of the great challenges of the next century.
"It will be necessary to show proof, in action, wisdom and vision, if we want to satisfy humanity's needs and avoid the most precious of natural resources becoming an object of conflict," he said.
